## The defect, reproduced by an executed probe

This adapter answers the question 'have we already talked to this person on LinkedIn' for a loop that sends cold outreach. It requests ONE page of /chats (limit 100) and reports coverage reached=True. The audit's probe planted a prior conversation beyond that first page: the adapter produced zero observations, the resolver returned NO_CONTACT_FOUND, and safe_for_cold_open came back true. A truncated read wearing a completeness receipt would have cleared a cold 'want to come on the show?' email to somebody mid-conversation with the owner — the exact incident this whole subsystem was built to prevent, reintroduced one layer down.

The governing rule, from the resolver's own docstring: not-looked-at is not the same as nothing-there. A page never fetched is a conversation never seen, so a partial read must NEVER be certified complete.

## What to change in _UnipileLinkedInClient.fetch and observe

1. PAGINATE. Unipile's GET /chats returns {"items": [...], "cursor": <opaque string or null>}. When a response carries a non-empty cursor, request the next page passing that cursor as the `cursor` query parameter alongside account_id and limit, and keep going until a response carries no cursor. Accumulate items across pages.

2. FAIL CLOSED ON PARTIAL READS. Two cases, both must end with the source reported reached=False and a one-line reason (exception class / HTTP status only — never a URL, query string, token or account id):
   a. any page request raises mid-pagination. Observations already gathered from earlier pages may still be returned — a touch that WAS seen still holds a candidate, that is the safe direction — but coverage must say the read did not complete;
   b. a sanity bound on pages (choose something generous, e.g. 100 pages) is hit while a cursor is still outstanding. Say pagination was not exhausted. Never loop unbounded.

3. THE SIMPLE CASE STAYS SIMPLE. One page with no cursor is a complete read: reached=True, exactly one request.

Keep everything else exactly as it is: the record normalisation from first_name/last_name, the credential handling in build_client (three env vars or the single JSON blob), the privacy rule that no message text leaves the adapter, and the observe()/map_records() contracts.

## The leak, demonstrated by an executed check

When a read fails, both adapters build their coverage detail from the RAW exception text (gmail_source.py around lines 114-120, hubspot_source.py around 146-152). The candidate feeder then writes that detail verbatim into its reasons receipt — an artifact whose contract is aliases only, no names, no addresses. A provider error routinely quotes the request that failed: an email address inside a query string, a full URL with parameters, sometimes a credential fragment. The executed check drove both adapters with such an exception and all three planted secrets (an address, a query string, a token) came back in the coverage detail.

One flaky HTTP call and a real person's address lands in a receipt nothing else was allowed to put it in.

## The rule

A coverage detail may carry exactly two things: the exception CLASS NAME, and the HTTP status code when one exists (urllib's HTTPError carries .code; an int embedded in provider text like 'HTTP Error 429' may also be recognised). A status number is not sensitive, and it separates retry-in-a-moment from never-going-to-work. The exception's own prose never travels. The linkedin adapter already does this — read its _one_line_error for the house pattern — and scripts/identity_proposals.py does the same; match them.

Apply the same rule to EVERY place in these two files that formats an exception into a detail string, including the build_client-unavailable path if it embeds anything dynamic.

Change nothing else: fetch logic, record shapes, credential handling, and observe()/map_records() behaviour all stay as they are.
